Working with others to generate ideas
Looking for patterns and making generalisation
Talking confidently and explaining ideas/opinions clearly
Using a range of media to communicate ideas
Using mathematics to justify and support decisions
Using technology to create, manipulate and process information

Respectfully responding to people of all cultures

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates cells and tissues, by analysing and relating their structure to function, as a basis for medical research in order to improve health.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the properties and functions of chemical compounds (water, lipids, proteins including enzymes from mammals) in a cell, focusing on their roles in maintaining cellular structure and metabolic processes in living organisms. (s, gs)
operate a light microscope to observe tissues from plants and animals under different magnifications. (s, gs)
analyse the ultrastructure of animal/ plant cells, bacterial cells, and the plasma membrane, to distinguish prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell characteristics. (s, gs)

analyse the structures of plant (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, and phloem) and animal (epithelial, cardiac, areolar, fibrous, and skeletal) tissues to assess their roles in physiological processes, disease diagnosis, and levels of organisation. (u, s, v/a, gs).

must_cover: interaction of water with polar and non-polar substances
simple and conjugated lipids, their properties, and functions
structural categories of proteins, their properties, and functions
mechanisms of enzyme action (Lock and key, induced fit hypothesis)
different types of enzyme inhibition
ultrastructure of animal/ plant cells, bacterial cells
fluid-mosaic model of the plasma membrane
prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
plant tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, and phloem
animal tissues: epithelial, cardiac, areolar, fibrous, and skeletal

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for and discuss: i) interaction of water with polar and non-polar substances. ii) simple and conjugated lipids, their properties, and functions. iii) structural categories of proteins, their properties, and functions. Create audio-visual presentations and share them with other groups.

Using modelling or dramatisation, learners discuss: i) the mechanisms of enzyme action. (Lock and key, induced fit hypothesis) ii) the different types of enzyme inhibition. Make a write-up and present it to the class in a plenary.

In groups, learners dissect a small mammal and extract structures that contain enzymes. Design and carry out scientific investigations on enzyme substrate specificity, effects of inhibitors, substrate, and enzyme concentrations on enzyme-controlled reactions, and write a scientific report.
In pairs, learners prepare slides, observe under low and medium power, and determine the linear magnification of the cells observed. Make a write-up and present findings to the class in a plenary.

In groups learners: i) study and compare images of ultra-structures of animal or plant cells with a bacterium cell, and make diagrams using a suitable graphics program. ii) study images of the fluid-mosaic model of the plasma membrane, make a model and use it to explain the functions of the membrane and its parts. Make a write-up and present the findings to the class.
Learners search and categorise the cells as prokaryotic and eukaryotic and present their work to the rest of the groups.

Learners search for the differences in the ultrastructure of prokaryotes, design an annotated flow diagram, and use it to explain the division of the original kingdom Monera to kingdoms eubacteria and archaebacteria.

In groups learners: i) observe and discuss micrographs, images, prepared slides, or prepared slides of plant tissues, epithelial tissues, and connective tissues. ii) relate the structure and location of the tissues to their functions. Make a write-up with labelled drawings and present it to the class.

In pairs, learners conduct an investigation to compare micrographs of healthy tissues from the internal organs (liver, lungs, heart, or intestines) of a mammal, with images of micrographs of diseased tissues from the same organs. Make a report and present the findings to the class.
Learners hold a debate titled 'Organisms at the organ level are more efficient than those at the cellular and tissue level'.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) sort and analyse information during the discussion. ii) work effectively in diverse teams when carrying out scientific investigations
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to: i) relate the properties of the chemical compounds to their functions. ii) explain the commercial application of enzyme inhibition.
Assess the learner’s: i) presentation/ write-up for correct science facts. ii) scientific reports for coherence in all the sections (title, aim, hypothesis, methods, results, and discussion).
Observe the learner’s ability to: i) prepare slides and use a microscope. ii) measure the field of view and estimate cell size.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to use a microscope to obtain results.
Assess the learner’s write-up for correct calculation of linear magnification.
Observe learners’ ability to: i) use the model to show the parts of plasma membrane and state their function. ii) use imagination to come up with unique models.

Probe learner’s to: i) identify the key differences in the structures of the cells. ii) explain the fluid-mosaic nature of the membrane. iii) mention the non-structural differences between eubacteria and archaebacteria.
Assess if the: i) categories formed show clarity and correctness of the differences between the cells. ii) models depict the structure and functionality of the plasma membrane.

Observe the learners’ ability to: i) analyse the structure and arrangement of cells in each tissue. ii) dissect and extract sample tissues from a rat. iii) identify the advantages of each level of organisation.

Use probing questions to find out the learner’s ability to: i) justify the unique features and location of the tissues. ii) distinguish features of the extracted tissue from the diseased one. iii) defend their views in a debate.
Assess the drawings if they depict the features of the different tissues.

practicals.title: Enzyme Investigation
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners dissect a small mammal and extract structures that contain enzymes. Design and carry out scientific investigations on enzyme substrate specificity, effects of inhibitors, substrate, and enzyme concentrations on enzyme-controlled reactions, and write a scientific report.

practicals.title: Microscopy: Tissues
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners prepare slides, observe under low and medium power, and determine the linear magnification of the cells observed.

practicals.title: Tissue Extraction and Analysis
practicals.description_verbatim: dissect and extract sample tissues from a rat.

investigative_skills.text_verbatim: Design and carry out scientific investigations
measure the field of view and estimate cell size

suggested_uses: make diagrams using a suitable graphics program

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates the nutritional strategies of carbon three (C3) and carbon four (C4) plants by analysing their photosynthetic pathways and adaptation to environmental conditions so as to optimise agricultural productivity and food security under varying climatic conditions.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: evaluate the relationship between the structure of chloroplast and photosynthesis in C3 and C4 plants (u, s, gs)
assess the influence of environmental factors on the photosynthetic efficiency of plants to optmise photosynthetic rates and crop yields. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: ultrastructure of a chloroplast
light-dependent and independent stages of photosynthesis in C3 and C4 plants
specific pathways involved in the synthesis of proteins and lipids, using intermediates (ATP, NADPH, G3P) of reactions of photosynthesis
behaviour of guard cells under varying sucrose concentrations

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners study images/tactile diagrams of the ultrastructure of a chloroplast, make a model, and use it to explain the functions of the parts.
Using role play, learners in their groups demonstrate the light-dependent and independent stages of photosynthesis in C3 and C4 plants.

In groups, learners search and discuss the specific pathways involved in the synthesis of proteins and lipids, using intermediates (ATP, NADPH, G3P) of reactions of photosynthesis. Using computer-generated infographics, learners present their findings to the rest of the class.
In groups, learners use project-based learning to design, build, and operate a mini-greenhouse.

In pairs, learners carry out scientific investigations on the behaviour of guard cells under varying sucrose concentrations. i) Learners write a report including relevant drawings. ii) Learners use their findings to explain the photosynthetic theory for the opening and closure of stomata.

In pairs, learners analyse data on the distribution and abundance of C3 and C4 plants at different altitudes, temperatures, and oxygen concentrations Using a presentation program, each pair presents their report and explanations in a class plenary session.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) work effectively in diverse teams during discussion and roleplay. ii) use technology to communicate and refine their presentations.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of: i) how the parts of the chloroplast suit their functions. ii) the advantages of C4 over C3 plants. iii) how plants form different products of photosynthesis.
Assess the learner’s presentations for the correct sequence of events in the processes.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) collaborate during the selection of suitable materials for the greenhouse. ii) Interrogate and interpret data on photosynthesis.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’: i) ability to explain the effect of water stress on the rate of photosynthesis. ii) the effect of light (intermittent and continuous) on the rate of photosynthesis. iii) ability to explain the relationship between varying sucrose concentration with stomatal opening/closing. iv) understanding of the efficiency of PEP carboxylase versus Rubisco.
Assess the learner’s reports for the application of greenhouse technologies and the accuracy of the scientific report.

practicals.title: Guard Cells Investigation
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners carry out scientific investigations on the behaviour of guard cells under varying sucrose concentrations. i) Learners write a report including relevant drawings.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners use project-based learning to design, build, and operate a mini-greenhouse.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates the mechanisms of transport of substances in the blood, and the immune system’s role in protecting the human body by analysing the processes and their role in the maintenance of human health, to prevent diseases in everyday life.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: assess the role of the human heart in blood circulation and the role of haemoglobin in the transportation of gases in blood under various physiological conditions. (u, s, gs, v/a)
analyse the role of antibodies in vaccination and allergic reactions in relation to human body immunity. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: transportation of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the body
effect of different factors on the amount of oxygen in the blood
effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the heartbeat rate
responses of athletes versus non-athletes
low-land dwellers versus high-land dwellers
carbon monoxide poisoning
myogenic action of the heart and nervous control of heartbeat rate
innate and adaptive immunity
concept of vaccination
role of histamine in allergy
new-born haemolytic disease
structure and action of antibodies
rapid test kits mechanism

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for: i) the transportation of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the body. ii) effect of different factors on the amount of oxygen in the blood. iii) the effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the heartbeat rate. iv) the responses of athletes versus non-athletes, and low-land dwellers versus high-land dwellers, to exercise. Learners discuss, create audio-visual presentations, and share with other groups.

In groups, learners are provided with case studies on carbon monoxide poisoning. They analyse to find out the problems and causes and propose strategies to prevent/manage the challenges. Learners make a write-up and present their findings to the other groups.

In groups, learners watch/listen to video clips/ animations or search on the myogenic action of the heart and nervous control of heartbeat rate. Learners discuss and make illustrations, present their work, and critique the group findings.

Learners search for and discuss: i) types of immunity (innate and adaptive). ii) the concept of vaccination. iii) role of histamine in allergy. iv) new-born haemolytic disease. In groups, learners make write-ups and present their work to the class plenary.

Learners search for the structure and action of antibodies, discuss and i) design antibody models, and create visual presentations to share with other groups. ii) Search for the mechanism used in rapid test kits to detect infections. In groups, learners make write-ups and present their work to the class plenary.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) share tasks and ideas. ii) create and use visual aids to illustrate their findings.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’: i) understanding of the importance of chloride shift in carbon dioxide transportation. ii) understanding of oxygen dissociation in the respiring tissue. iii) ability to explain the effect of carbon monoxide on transportation of oxygen. iv) understanding of the role played by the brain, sinoatrial node, and atrioventricular node during regulation of the heartbeat.
Assess the visual aids for the correct representation of the concepts of transport of gases.
Observe the learners' ability to: i) work effectively in diverse teams. ii) sort and analyse. iii) information about vaccination. iv) use models to represent the structure of the antibody.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’: i) understanding of non-specific and specific body defence mechanisms. ii) ability to explain the action of antibodies. iii) ability to describe the effects of histamine. iv) understanding of the effect of Rhesus compatibility of couples on the baby.
Assess the clarity of learner’s models, and visual presentations for the right sequence of events that occur during body defense and report for correctness of information.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates how living organisms generate cellular energy, by analysing respiratory processes and the chemical breakdown of food within cells, to make informed decisions that promote good health and wellbeing.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: examine the relationship between the structure of the mitochondrion and the stages of cellular respiration in living organisms. (u, s)
analyse the biochemical processes leading to ATP production in living organisms, and how these processes are affected by physical activities and respiratory poisons (cyanide). (u, s, gs, v/a).

must_cover: ultrastructure of a mitochondrion
hydrolysis of Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
glycolysis
role of acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA)
citric acid cycle (substrate-level phosphorylation, decarboxylation, NADH, FADH2)
oxidative phosphorylation
electron transport chain (protein complexes, NADH, FADH2, oxygen)
effect of cyanide on electron transport system
ATP production during various exercise intensities

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners study images of the ultrastructure of a mitochondrion, make drawings, and share them in a class plenary.

Learners individually search for and discuss the structural relationship of the mitochondrion to its functions and hydrolysis of Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to release energy. Using concept mapping, learners present their work in a class plenary.

In groups, learners use simulations that demonstrate the process of glycolysis, focusing on its stages, key molecules involved, and its significance in cellular respiration. Make a write-up and present it to the class plenary.

Using the jigsaw strategy, learners discuss the role of acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) in the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins. Each group creates a summary chart showing the integration of these pathways through acetyl-CoA and presents it to the class.

In groups, learners search for the citric acid cycle, focusing on key steps (substrate-level phosphorylation, decarboxylation, and the production of NADH and FADH₂). Groups then engage in a hands-on activity, such as constructing a flowchart, to visualise the cycle and present it in class.

In groups, learners search for oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondrion. Learners watch a video clip or role-play the events of electron transport focusing on the role of protein complexes, NADH, FADH2, and oxygen. Make a write-up and present.
Learners search for or watch an animation explaining how cyanide disrupts the electron transport system. They then pair up to share and present their findings.
In groups, learners search for how ATP production changes during various exercise intensities. Learners make write-ups and use gallery walks to discuss their findings.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) listen, and equally contribute to the discussions. ii) Sort and analyse information related to the structures in a mitochondrion and their functions.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of: i) the detailed structure. ii) energy release from ATP.
Assess the learners’ concept map for the correct relationship between structure and function.

Observe the learners’ ability to: i) listen, equally contribute to the discussions, and build on each other’s ideas. ii) use visual or physical items to represent the sequence of reactions and the role of key molecules.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of: i) key steps involved in the sugar breakdown in the cytoplasm. ii) the central role of acetyl-CoA in metabolism. iii) the fate of Acetyl-CoA, NAD, and FAD. iv) cyanide effect on the electron transport system. v) the exercise intensity on ATP production.
Assess learners’ presentations for the correct sequence of events.

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates the regulation and maintenance of optimal internal environment in living organisms by analysing how organ systems generate and eliminate metabolic wastes and maintain the functioning of cells, to make life choices that promote wellness.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the homeostatic control system, focusing on the role of negative feedback mechanisms in maintaining internal stability. (u, s, gs)

examine the adaptations and management of different plant categories (xerophytes, mesophytes, and hydrophytes) based on their osmoregulatory abilities and the application of excretory plant products in everyday life. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: significance of maintaining a stable internal environment
components of an efficient homeostatic system
physiological and behavioural adaptations of endotherms
role of the hypothalamus and skin in regulating temperature in endotherms
how ADH works to maintain water balance
animal adaptations to different water availability
plant adaptations to varying water availability (xerophytes, mesophytes, hydrophytes)
excretory products in plants (latex, anthocyanins, oils, quinine, and saponins)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for i) the significance of maintaining a stable internal environment. ii) components of an efficient homeostatic system. Make a write-up and share their findings with the class.

In groups, learners use mind maps to: i) illustrate the physiological and behavioural adaptations of endotherms to survive in varying temperature conditions. ii) illustrate the role of the hypothalamus and skin in regulating temperature in endotherms. Groups present their mind maps to the rest of the class through a gallery walk.
In groups, learners describe how ADH works to maintain water balance in the body. Make a write-up and present it in a class plenary.
Using Socratic circles, learners analyse and discuss animal adaptations to different water availability in their environment. Make a write-up and present it in a class plenary.

In pairs, learners search for and discuss: i) plant adaptations to varying water availability in their habitats. ii) techniques employed by humans to manage plants that survive in different environments. Learners create illustrations using a suitable computer program and present their work.
Using the project-based learning method, learners investigate excretory products in plants (latex, anthocyanins, oils, quinine, and saponins) to discover their uses in everyday life.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners' ability to: i) share information about how a homeostatic system works. ii) work together as they create visual illustrations.

Use probing questions to find out the learner’s understanding of: i) the effect of varying the internal environment. ii) role of the homeostatic system. iii) the role of thermal receptors and the hypothalamus. iv) mechanisms to manage water stress.
Assess the learners’presentations for accuracy of scientific facts.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) form ideas and make visual illustrations. ii) plan and execute project activities.
Use probing questions to assess the learners’ ability to: i) classify plants according to water requirements. ii) harness excretory products from plants.
Assess the learners’write-ups for management strategies and exploitation of plant excretory products.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Using the project-based learning method, learners investigate excretory products in plants (latex, anthocyanins, oils, quinine, and saponins) to discover their uses in everyday life.

suggested_uses: create illustrations using a suitable computer program
